title: Jerusalem falls (2 Kings 25)
hook: the temple burned, the people carried to Babylon
carry: even exile is not the end

segments.voice: Yesterday, Josiah, told the book of the law was found in the temple during repairs. Your line was the book was lost in the house. What did you pick up and reread? Day seven hundred thirty-nine.
screen: `THE BOOK WAS LOST IN THE HOUSE.`

segments.voice: "By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion." That's a psalm, and it's sung by people a very long way from home. How did they get there? The answer is in a hard chapter at the end of Second Kings. An army from Babylon surrounds Jerusalem. The siege goes on until there is no bread left in the city. The wall is broken through. The king, Zedekiah, runs for it by night and is caught near Jericho. And then the Babylonian commander comes to the city with fire. Today's word is what came next for a whole people.

The King James Bible tells it flatly, almost like an inventory: "he burnt the house of the LORD, and the king's house, and all the houses of Jerusalem, and every great man's house burnt he with fire." The temple Solomon prayed in, gone. The walls pulled down. The bronze pillars broken up and carried off as scrap. Then the people. The rest of the city is carried away to Babylon, and the poorest are left behind to tend the vines and the fields. The chapter sums it up in one line: "So Judah was carried away out of their land." That's exile: not just moving, but being taken from the place where your God's house stood, to a city where everything says your story is over. And here's what's worth noticing. The writer of Kings could have stopped there. The burning is the obvious ending. But the chapter keeps going. Years later in Babylon, a new king lets the old exiled king of Judah, Jehoiachin, out of prison. And the text says: "he spake kindly to him." He gives him new clothes instead of prison garments, and a seat at the king's table, every day, for the rest of his life. That's the last scene of the whole book. Not a rescue. Not a return home. Just a man in exile, eating at a table, spoken to kindly. Some readers hear in it a small sign that the line of David isn't finished. Others simply hear that the story kept going. And the psalm from the opening is sung from inside that exile, by the rivers of Babylon. A people who lost their land did not lose their voice.

Here's the practice: remember people far from home. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind people who've lost their homeland: refugees in the news, a family that moved to your street, a coworker who can't go back, maybe your own grandparents. Don't try to solve anything. Picture one face, or one family, at their kitchen table tonight, a long way from where they started. If you pray, you can pray for them in your own words, by name if you know it. If you don't, just hold them in mind for the length of the bell. The bell holds the time.
Exile. Being carried away from your land, as Judah was taken to Babylon when Jerusalem fell and the temple burned.
Your line: even exile is not the end. Today, speak kindly to one person who is far from home, the way a king once did in Babylon. Day seven hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Christians read the fall of Jerusalem and the exile in Bible readings and sermons, sometimes alongside Psalm 137 and the prophets, and some churches pray for refugees and displaced people when these passages come up.

fork.setup: you're writing the history of your people, and you've just told how the temple burned and the people were carried away. how do you end the book?
options: with the fire. there's nothing left to say.
with a lament for everything lost.
with the exiled king spoken to kindly and given a seat at the table.
fork.reveal: 2 Kings ends with Jehoiachin out of prison, in new clothes, eating at the king's table. not a return home, but not the end of the story.

original.note: Hebrew: exile, being carried away from the land.

trapdoor: what you thought: the fall of Jerusalem is where the story ends.
what it means: the temple burns and the people are carried away, but the book closes on a captive king spoken to kindly.
what a scholar hears: the last verses of 2 Kings (25:27–30) give a release from prison, new clothes and a daily place at the table, and some readers hear the line of David still alive.

notes: 'The rest of the city is carried away' paraphrases 25:11; confirm.
'The temple Solomon prayed in' links to day 732 (1 Kings 8); confirm.
'Some of the Psalms and prophets come from those years' is a general claim (Psalm 137 is set there); confirm or soften.
The reading of 25:27–30 as a hint that David's line continues is attributed to 'some readers'.
Original: גָּלוּת (galut) is the later Jewish term for exile; 2 Kings 25:21 uses the verb גָּלָה. Confirm the note.
Practice: free prayer in one's own words is invited, not written.

Editor pass: superlative 'one of the hardest chapters in the Bible' cut; unsourced claims that 'some of the Psalms and prophets come from those years' and that Jews and Christians 'both' wrote from inside the exile (Christians did not yet exist) replaced by the cited Psalm 137; Original note no longer generalizes about what 'Jews use'.

Audit: 'the book goes on a few more verses' / 'ends a few verses later' understated the gap (the burning is 25:9; the book ends at 25:30, after the Gedaliah episode, 25:22–26); now 'the chapter keeps going' / 'later in the chapter'. Note above citing day 732 for Solomon's prayer should read day 728.
